en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga,
Chapter on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Robes 8.
The Training Rule on What Has Been Prepared.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a certain man said this to his wife:
"I will clothe the venerable Upananda with a robe.
A certain monk who was wandering for alms heard these words being spoken by that man.
Then that bhikkhu approached the Venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta; having approached, he said this to the Venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta:
"You are one of great merit, friend Upananda.
In such-and-such a place, a certain man said this to his wife:"
“I will clothe the venerable Upananda with a robe.
“Indeed, friend, he is my attendant.
Then the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan-son went to that man; having approached him, he said this to that man:
“Is it true, friend, that you wish to clothe me with a robe?
“It is indeed so for me, sir:
‘I shall clothe the venerable Upananda with a robe.’”
“If you wish to clothe me with a robe, friend, clothe me with such a robe as this.
What shall I do with it, even if I am clothed in it, since I will not use it?
Then that man complained, grumbled, and became indignant.
“These recluses, sons of the Sakyan, have great desires and are not content.
It will not be easy to clothe them with robes.
How indeed could the venerable Upananda, without being previously invited by me, approach me and make a request regarding a robe?”
The monks heard that man grumbling, complaining, and criticizing.
Those monks who were few in desires... [as before] ...they grumbled, complained, and criticized, saying:
"How can the Venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta, without having been previously invited, approach a householder and make a request for a robe?"
Then those bhikkhus, having rebuked the Venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One. … [The Blessed One asked:
“Is it true, Upananda, that you previously approached a householder who had not invited you and made a request for robe-cloth?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
“Upananda, is he a relative of yours or not?
“He is not a relative, Blessed One.
“An unrelated person, foolish man, does not know what is appropriate or inappropriate, or what is real or unreal, regarding another unrelated person.”
"In that case, you fool of a man, how could you approach an unrelated householder without being previously invited and enter into a request for robe-cloth?
This, fool of a man, will not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...

And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows: ‘If a monk, without being previously invited by a householder or his wife, should approach them and enter into a request for robe-cloth, saying: “Friends, it would be good if you were to provide me with robe-cloth from this set of cloth-materials,” then, unless it has been previously arranged, that is a *nissaggiya pācittiya*.’”
“Now, suppose a robe-fund has been set aside by an unrelated householder or housewife for the sake of a certain bhikkhu, [thinking]:
‘Having purchased a robe with this robe-fund, we shall clothe the bhikkhu named so-and-so with a robe.
If that bhikkhu, not having been previously invited, should go there and make a specific choice regarding the robe:”
‘It would be good indeed if the venerable one, having purchased such and such a robe with this robe-fund, would clothe me in it,’ out of a desire for something fine—
this is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
“But [regarding the phrase] ‘having designated a monk’...”
"For the sake of a bhikkhu" means: having made a bhikkhu the object, desiring to clothe a bhikkhu.
"A stranger" means:
one who is not related on the mother's side or the father's side, up to the seventh generation of ancestors.
A householder is anyone who dwells in a home.
A housewife is...
Whoever dwells in a household.
What is called "cloth-money" (cīvaracetāpanna) is either gold or silver, or pearls, or gems, or coral, or crystal, or cloth, or thread, or cotton.
"By this robe-fund" means by that which has been set aside. "Having caused it to be purchased" means...
Having exchanged [it],
[thinking] "I shall clothe [him]," I will give it.
"In that case, 'that monk' refers to the monk for whose sake the robe-fund has been prepared.
'Without having been previously invited' means— "
It was not previously asked: "Venerable sir, what kind of robe do you need? What kind of robe shall I have made for you?
"Having approached" means having gone to the house, or having approached anyone at all.
"To make a choice regarding the robe-cloth" means:
"Whether it be long, or wide, or fine, or soft;
with this robe-fund."
Presented as:
"of such a kind or of such a kind," whether long, broad, thick, or fine.
"Cetāpetvā" means having exchanged.
"Acchādehi" means clothe [him].
"May you give.
"Out of a desire for what is wholesome" means:
one who seeks excellence, one who seeks high value.
If, at his word, he causes [cloth] to be obtained that is long, wide, thick, or fine, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the effort.
With the acquisition, it becomes subject to relinquishment (nissaggiya).
It must be relinquished to the Saṅgha, or to a group, or to an individual.
And thus, monks, it should be relinquished:
“… ‘Venerable sir, this robe-cloth, which I previously approached an unrelated householder about without being invited, and for which I made a choice regarding the robe, is to be relinquished.’”
“I relinquish this to the Saṅgha.
… “He should give it” … “They should give it” … [and so on].
"I give it to the Venerable One.

If, regarding one who is unknown, he perceives them as unknown, and having approached a householder without being previously invited, he makes a specification concerning a robe, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.

If, regarding one who is unknown, he is doubtful, and having approached a householder without being previously invited, he makes a specification concerning a robe, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.

If, perceiving one who is unrelated as related, he approaches a householder who has not previously invited him and makes a request regarding a robe, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If he perceives one who is related as unrelated, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If he is in doubt regarding one who is related, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one perceives a relative as a relative, there is no offense. There is no offense in the case of relatives.
When [the monks] have been invited,
for the sake of another,
with one's own wealth.
If one who wishes to have something of great value exchanged obtains something of little value;
or if he is insane;
or if he is a first-time offender.
The eighth training rule concerning what has been prepared is finished.
